'''''Setaria palmifolia''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the common names '''palmgrass''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SEPA6|taxon=Setaria palmifolia|accessdate=11 November 2015}}</ref> '''highland pitpit''', '''hailans pitpit''', '''short pitpit''', '''broadleaved bristlegrass''', and '''knotroot'''.

==Description==
This species is a perennial grass with stems growing up to {{Convert|2 or 3|m|ft|frac=2}}<ref name=china>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200026275 ''Setaria palmifolia''.] Flora of China.</ref><ref name=kew>[http://www.kew.org/data/grasses-db/www/imp09398.htm ''Setaria palmifolia''.] GrassBase - The Online World Grass Flora. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.</ref> long from a knotty [[rhizome]]. The stems can be up to 1 centimetre thick. The leaf sheaths are sparsely<ref name=china/> to totally hairy.<ref name=kew/> The leaf blades are linear, oval,<ref name=kew/> or lance-shaped and up to {{Convert|60 to 80|cm|abbr=on}}<ref name=china/><ref name=kew/> long by 7 or 8 cm wide. They have a pleated texture and are hairless or with some rough hairs.

The [[panicle]] is loose, open and spreading, reaching up to 80 cm long. The spikelet is a few millimetres long but is often accompanied by a bristle which can be 1.5 cm long.<ref name="china" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is native to [[Temperate climate|temperate]] and [[tropics|tropical]] Asia.<ref name="grin">{{GRIN|accessdate=21 January 2018}}</ref> It is known elsewhere as an [[introduced species|introduced]], and often [[invasive species|invasive]], species, including in Australia, New Zealand, many [[Pacific Islands]],<ref name="pier">[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/setaria_palmifolia.htm ''Setaria palmifolia''.] Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER). USDA Forest Service.</ref> and the Americas.<ref name="grin" />

== Ecology ==
The grass has been introduced to many areas, often as an ornamental. It is widespread in the Pacific Islands. It has become an invasive plant on [[Lord Howe Island]], [[Norfolk Island]], [[Rapa Nui]], [[Fiji]], and the [[Solomon Islands]], and in [[Samoa]] and [[Hawaii]]. It is also invasive in New Zealand and [[Queensland]].<ref name="pier" />

The grass is robust and spreads via rhizome and seed banks, forming monotypic stands. It is a tall plant with wide leaves that shade out other vegetation.<ref name="pier" /> The rampant feral pigs of Hawaii facilitate its spread there by uprooting the surrounding plants while feeding on its thick stems. It is also spread by [[seed predation|seed-eating]] birds.<ref name="hi">[http://www.botany.hawaii.edu/faculty/cw_smith/set_pal.htm ''Setaria palmifolia''.] Pest Plants of Hawaiian Native Ecosystems. Department of Botany, University of Hawaii at Manoa.</ref>

This species is host to the [[fungus|fungi]] ''[[Cercospora setariae]]'' and ''[[Phacellium paspali]]''.<ref name="fungi">Kirschner, R., et al. (2004). [http://www.fungaldiversity.org/fdp/sfdp/17-5.pdf Some cercosporoid hyphomycetes from Taiwan, including a new species of ''Stenella'' and new reports of ''Distocercospora pachyderma'' and ''Phacellium paspali''.] ''Fungal Diversity'' 17, 57-68.</ref>

== Uses ==
The grass is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for its palm-like pleated leaves. Some [[cultivar]]s have striped leaves and 'Rubra' has purple midribs.<ref name=flori>[http://www.floridata.com/ref/s/seta_pal.cfm A Floridata Plant Profile: ''Setaria palmifolia''.] FloriData.</ref>

It is grown as a [[vegetable]] crop in [[Papua New Guinea]], where that is known as highland pitpit. The stem of the grass is eaten after cooking.<ref name=rose>Rose, C. J. (1980). [http://www.cabdirect.org/abstracts/19826740480.html Optimum replanting stage for two varieties of pit-pit (''Setaria palmifolia'') in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea.] ''Papua New Guinea Agricultural Journal'' 31(1-4), 23-29.</ref> The grain can be eaten as a [[rice]] substitute.<ref name=gm>[http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Setaria_palmifolia&type=treatment ''Setaria palmifolia''.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304113520/http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Setaria_palmifolia&type=treatment |date=2016-03-04 }} Grass Manual. Flora of North America.</ref>

==In culture==
A folk belief in Taiwan holds that the number of latitudinal creases on the leaf predicts the number of typhoons that will hit the area in the coming or current typhoon season. It is known locally as '''typhoon grass'''.
